title: Ötzi the Iceman’s Ancient Yeast Bakes a Tasty Loaf, and Google’s 64-Million-Mosquito Plan
summary:
Talk about a long fermentation! Scientists have successfully baked bread using yeast harvested from Ötzi the Iceman, the 5,300-year-old mummy discovered in the Italian Alps in 1991. Ötzi’s naturally mummified body was infiltrated by cold-adapted glacier yeasts shortly after his death — and incredibly, those microbes may still be active today. Researchers isolated four strains and, in a delicious twist, used them to make sourdough. Their verdict? 'Very very good.' It’s a quirky blend of archaeology and baking that gives new meaning to 'ancient grains.'

But the past wasn’t the only thing making headlines. In Italy, a group of teenagers stumbled upon an 1,800-year-old Roman villa hidden beneath their high school gym — a surprise discovery that turned their campus into an archaeological site overnight. Meanwhile, in the U.K., scientists documented 17,000-year-old rock art, now the oldest ever recorded in the country. And on the high seas, researchers identified the first shipwrecks linked to the real pirates of the Caribbean.

In a story that sounds like science fiction, Google has applied to the Environmental Protection Agency for a permit to release 64 million male southern house mosquitoes across the U.S. These mosquitoes are non-biting and infected with Wolbachia pipientis, a bacterium that makes them sterile. When they mate with wild females, the resulting eggs don’t hatch, causing mosquito populations to plummet. Since female southern house mosquitoes transmit diseases like West Nile virus and St. Louis encephalitis, the plan could significantly reduce illness. The EPA considers the request potentially significant and will decide after a public comment period that ended June 5.

On a sadder note, NASA declared its MAVEN spacecraft at Mars officially 'unrecoverable' on June 3. The probe lost contact in December 2025 after a routine pass behind the planet. A review board found that a rapid rotation likely drained its batteries. MAVEN had been studying the Martian atmosphere since 2014. Its loss closes a chapter, but the data it sent back will fuel discoveries for years.
why_it_matters: This news shows how ancient life can still affect our modern world — from food to medicine — and how carefully controlled technology can help solve big public health problems like mosquito-borne diseases.

background_read: Ötzi the Iceman is one of the oldest and best-preserved natural mummies ever found. His body was discovered in 1991 by hikers in the Ötztal Alps on the border between Italy and Austria. He lived around 3300 BCE, during the Copper Age, and his remains have given scientists incredible insights into the life of prehistoric Europeans.

The use of yeast in breadmaking dates back thousands of years. Ancient Egyptians were among the first to intentionally use fermentation to make leavened bread. The yeast in Ötzi’s case is not human-added but came from the cold glacier environment that infiltrated his body after death. This shows how microbes can survive extreme conditions for millennia.

Wolbachia pipientis is a bacterium that naturally infects many insect species. Scientists have been using a technique called the Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) for decades to control pests, like the screwworm fly, by releasing sterile males. The mosquito plan proposed by Google’s parent company Alphabet (through its subsidiary Verily) uses a refined version of this idea to fight diseases like Zika, dengue, and West Nile virus.

The EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) is a U.S. federal agency that regulates the release of organisms into the environment to ensure public safety. Before an experiment like releasing millions of genetically modified mosquitoes can proceed, the EPA must evaluate potential risks and allow the public to comment.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A quirky science-meets-food story — baking bread with 5,300-year-old yeast from Ötzi the Iceman.
└─ specific: 'Very very good' verdict on the sourdough.
OTHER DISCOVERIES: A quick parade of historical finds — Roman villa under a school, 17,000-year-old rock art, first pirate shipwrecks recorded.
└─ TIMELINE: Ranges from 1,800 to 17,000 years ago.

├─ HOW: Infect males with Wolbachia pipientis to make them sterile.
├─ WHY: To reduce diseases like West Nile virus and St. Louis encephalitis.
└─ REGULATORY STEP: EPA permit process with public comment until June 5.
CLOSING NOTE: A sad update — MAVEN spacecraft at Mars lost after 11 years of studying the atmosphere.
└─ RESULT: Data continues to fuel discoveries, even though the probe is unrecoverable.

perspectives.perspective: Positive: Archaeology and food science benefit
perspectives.description: Using ancient yeast connects us to our ancestors and could spark new interest in food science and history. It’s a fun, tasty example of how scientific curiosity can lead to unexpected discoveries that enrich our culture and diet.

perspectives.perspective: Negative: Environmental and ethical risks of mosquito release
perspectives.description: Releasing millions of genetically modified organisms into the wild raises concerns about unintended effects on ecosystems. Some worry that eliminating a whole disease-carrying mosquito species might harm animals that eat them, or that the bacteria could spread in unexpected ways.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / Analytical: Scientific persistence and limitation
perspectives.description: The MAVEN loss shows even advanced technology has a lifespan, and space exploration involves constant trade-offs between risk and reward. The mosquito plan illustrates a well-established pest-control concept being updated with genetic tools — a pattern of human ingenuity applied to old problems.

The EPA’s decision could set a precedent for future insect-control projects, opening the door to larger-scale interventions against diseases. Meanwhile, the archaeological finds remind us that Earth still hides countless historical treasures, and the next big discovery might be just under our feet.
